question: According to the New Mexico CDL manual, what is the key difference between cargo tanks and portable tanks?
choice_a: Cargo tanks are permanently attached to a vehicle and remain on it when loaded and unloaded, while portable tanks are off the vehicle when loaded or unloaded
choice_b: Cargo tanks only carry gases, while portable tanks only carry liquids
choice_c: Portable tanks require placards, while cargo tanks never do
choice_d: Cargo tanks are used only for hazardous waste, while portable tanks carry only non-hazardous cargo
explanation: The manual states cargo tanks are bulk packaging permanently attached to a vehicle and remain on it during loading and unloading, while portable tanks are not permanently attached and are loaded or unloaded while off the vehicle.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5 Bulk Packaging Marking, Loading and Unloading

question: Identification numbers for hazardous materials in portable tanks and cargo tanks are found in which column of the Hazardous Materials Table?
choice_a: Column 4
choice_b: Column 1
choice_c: Column 2
choice_d: Column 3
explanation: The manual states that identification numbers are found in column 4 of the Hazardous Materials Table.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5.1 Markings

question: What markings are required for bulk packaging identification numbers when no placards are required?
choice_a: Black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers on orange panels, placards, or a white, diamond-shaped background
choice_b: Any color numbers as long as they are at least six inches tall
choice_c: Red numbers on a blue background
choice_d: No markings are required if placards are absent
explanation: The rules require black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers on orange panels, placards, or a white, diamond-shaped background if no placards are required.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5.1 Markings

question: On a portable tank with a capacity of more than 1,000 gallons, how tall must the letters of the shipping name be?
choice_a: At least two inches
choice_b: At least four inches
choice_c: At least one inch
choice_d: At least six inches
explanation: The manual specifies that the letters of the shipping name must be at least two inches tall on portable tanks with capacities of more than 1,000 gallons.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5.1 Markings

question: On a portable tank with a capacity of less than 1,000 gallons, how tall must the letters of the shipping name be at minimum?
choice_a: One inch
choice_b: Three inches
choice_c: Four inches
choice_d: Half an inch
explanation: The manual states the shipping name letters must be at least one inch tall on portable tanks with capacities of less than 1,000 gallons.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5.1 Markings

question: Where must the identification number appear on a portable tank holding 1,000 gallons or more?
choice_a: On the underside of the tank only
choice_b: On each side and each end of the tank
choice_c: Only on the rear of the tank
choice_d: It is not required if the shipping name is displayed
explanation: The manual requires the identification number to appear on each side and each end of a portable tank or other bulk packaging that holds 1,000 gallons or more; tanks holding less than 1,000 gallons need it on two opposing sides.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5.1 Markings

question: According to the manual, what is true about intermediate bulk containers (IBCs) regarding markings?
choice_a: They must display the driver's license number
choice_b: They must be painted a specific hazard color
choice_c: They are bulk packages but are not required to have the owner's name or shipping name
choice_d: They require the same two-inch lettering as all portable tanks over 1,000 gallons
explanation: The manual states that intermediate bulk containers (IBCs) are bulk packages, but are not required to have the owner's name or shipping name.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5.1 Markings

question: The person watching the loading or unloading of a cargo tank must be within how many feet of the tank?
choice_a: 100 feet
choice_b: 50 feet
choice_c: 10 feet
choice_d: 25 feet
explanation: The manual requires the person watching the loading or unloading to be alert, have a clear view of the cargo tank, and be within 25 feet of the tank.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5.2 Tank Loading

question: Before moving a tank of hazardous materials, no matter how small the amount, what must be done to the manholes and valves?
choice_a: Leave them open for ventilation
choice_b: Cover them with a tarp but they may remain open
choice_c: Close all manholes and valves
choice_d: Only close the manholes; valves may remain open
explanation: The manual requires closing all manholes and valves before moving a tank of hazardous materials, no matter how small the amount, to prevent leaks.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5.2 Tank Loading

question: Under 49 CFR 173.29, when is it legal to move a cargo tank with open valves or covers?
choice_a: Only on private property
choice_b: Only if the tank is empty
choice_c: Only during daylight hours
choice_d: Never, under any circumstance
explanation: The manual states it is illegal to move a cargo tank with open valves or covers unless it is empty according to 49 CFR 173.29.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5.2 Tank Loading

question: Before loading or unloading flammable liquids, what should you do with your engine?
choice_a: Leave it running at idle at all times
choice_b: Turn it off, running it only if needed to operate a pump
choice_c: Rev the engine to charge the battery
choice_d: Turn it off and disconnect the battery
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to turn off the engine before loading or unloading flammable liquids, only running it if needed to operate a pump.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5.3 Flammable Liquids

question: When filling a cargo tank of flammable liquid through an open filling hole, what grounding procedure must you follow?
choice_a: Ground the tank before opening the filling hole and maintain the ground until after closing it
choice_b: Grounding is only required for tanks over 5,000 gallons
choice_c: Ground the tank only after the filling hole is closed
choice_d: No grounding is required if the driver wears rubber-soled boots
explanation: The manual states you must ground a cargo tank correctly before filling it, grounding the tank before opening the filling hole and maintaining the ground until after closing the filling hole.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5.3 Flammable Liquids

question: Except when loading and unloading, how must liquid discharge valves on a compressed gas tank be kept?
choice_a: Partially open
choice_b: Removed entirely
choice_c: Closed
choice_d: Open
explanation: The manual states to keep liquid discharge valves on a compressed gas tank closed except when loading and unloading.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5.4 Compressed Gas

question: What must you always do to trailers and semi-trailers to prevent motion when they are uncoupled from the power unit during compressed gas transfer?
choice_a: Leave the engine running
choice_b: Chock them
choice_c: Fill their tanks completely first
choice_d: Cover them with a fire-resistant tarp
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to always chock trailers and semi-trailers to prevent motion when uncoupled from the power unit.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.5.4 Compressed Gas

question: Under the Do Not Load table, what is the rule for loading Division 6.1 or 2.3 (POISON or poison inhalation hazard) labeled material with animal or human food?
choice_a: It may never be loaded in the same vehicle under any circumstance
choice_b: It is allowed only if the poison package is over-packed in an approved way; note that mouthwash, toothpaste, and skin creams are not considered foodstuffs
choice_c: It is always allowed as long as the food is sealed in plastic
choice_d: It is allowed only for shipments under 50 pounds
explanation: The Do Not Load Table states poison or poison-inhalation-hazard labeled material cannot be loaded with animal or human food unless the poison package is over-packed in an approved way; the manual notes foodstuffs are anything you swallow, but mouthwash, toothpaste, and skin creams are not foodstuff.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, Do Not Load Table (Figure 9.9)

question: According to the Do Not Load table, Division 2.3 (Poisonous) gas Zone A or Division 6.1 (Poison) liquids, PGI, Zone A must not be loaded in the same vehicle with which of the following?
choice_a: Division 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 Explosives, Division 5.1 Oxidizers, Class 3 Flammable Liquids, and Class 8 Corrosive Liquids
choice_b: Only empty containers
choice_c: Non-hazardous general freight
choice_d: Class 9 miscellaneous hazardous materials only
explanation: The Do Not Load Table lists Division 1.1, 1.2, 1.3 Explosives, Division 5.1 Oxidizers, Class 3 Flammable Liquids, Class 8 Corrosive Liquids, Division 5.2 Organic Peroxides, Division 1.5 Blasting Agents, Division 2.1 Flammable Gases, and Class 4 Flammable Solids as materials that cannot be loaded with Division 2.3 Zone A gas or Division 6.1 PGI Zone A liquids.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, Do Not Load Table (Figure 9.9)

question: Per the Do Not Load table, charged storage batteries must not be loaded in the same vehicle with which hazard class?
choice_a: Division 1.1 Explosives
choice_b: Class 9 Miscellaneous
choice_c: Class 8 Corrosives
choice_d: Combustible liquids
explanation: The Do Not Load Table specifies that charged storage batteries must not be loaded in the same vehicle with Division 1.1 explosives.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, Do Not Load Table (Figure 9.9)

question: According to the Do Not Load table, Class 1 detonating primers must not be loaded with any other explosives unless what condition is met?
choice_a: The vehicle is placarded on all four sides
choice_b: They are in authorized containers or packages
choice_c: The trip is less than 50 miles
choice_d: A police escort is arranged
explanation: The Do Not Load Table states that Class 1 (Detonating primers) must not be loaded with any other explosives unless they are in authorized containers or packages.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, Do Not Load Table (Figure 9.9)

question: The Do Not Load table prohibits loading Division 6.1 cyanides or cyanide mixtures, such as Silver Cyanide and Sodium Cyanide, with which materials?
choice_a: Wood products
choice_b: Electronics
choice_c: Acids, corrosive materials, or other acidic materials which could release hydrocyanic acid
choice_d: Empty drums
explanation: The Do Not Load Table lists acids, corrosive materials, or other acidic materials that could release hydrocyanic acid as prohibited co-loads with Division 6.1 cyanides or cyanide mixtures such as Silver Cyanide and Sodium Cyanide.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, Do Not Load Table (Figure 9.9)

question: Per the Do Not Load table, nitric acid (Class 8) may be loaded with other materials only if what condition is met?
choice_a: The nitric acid is not loaded above any other material
choice_b: The other materials are also acids
choice_c: The nitric acid container is glass, not metal
choice_d: The shipment weighs less than 100 pounds
explanation: The Do Not Load Table states other materials cannot be loaded with nitric acid unless the nitric acid is not loaded above any other material.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, Do Not Load Table (Figure 9.9)

question: When loading corrosive liquids by hand, what precaution does the manual require for breakable containers?
choice_a: Load them two by two, side by side
choice_b: Load them one by one, keeping them right side up, without dropping or rolling
choice_c: Stack them upside down to prevent spills from the cap
choice_d: Load them only after wrapping in plastic sheeting
explanation: The manual instructs that if loading by hand, breakable containers of corrosive liquid should be loaded one by one, keeping them right side up, without dropping or rolling them, and loaded onto an even floor surface.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.4 Precautions for Specific Hazards (Corrosive Materials)

question: According to the manual, what is the maximum total transport index of all Class 7 (Radioactive) packages allowed in a single vehicle?
explanation: The manual states the total transport index of all Class 7 radioactive packages in a single vehicle must not exceed 50.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.4 Precautions for Specific Hazards (Radioactive Materials)

question: Where must you never load a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD?
choice_a: In the trailer's rear compartment
choice_b: In the driver's cab or sleeper, or with food material for human or animal consumption
choice_c: On a flatbed trailer
choice_d: Near the fuel tank
explanation: The manual states you must never load a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD in the driver's cab or sleeper or with food material for human or animal consumption.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.4 Precautions for Specific Hazards (Radioactive/Poison Materials)

question: While behind the wheel, where should hazardous materials shipping papers be kept?
choice_a: Locked in the glove compartment
choice_b: In the sleeper berth
choice_c: Within your reach with your seat belt on, or in a pouch on the driver's door
choice_d: In the trailer with the cargo
explanation: The manual states that when behind the wheel, keep shipping papers within your reach with your seat belt on, or in a pouch on the driver's door, so they are easily seen by someone entering the cab.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.10 Where to Keep Shipping Papers and Emergency Response Information

question: When not behind the wheel, where should shipping papers be left?
choice_a: Anywhere in the cab
choice_b: With the dispatcher by fax
choice_c: Under the passenger seat only
choice_d: In the driver's door pouch or on the driver's seat
explanation: The manual states that when not behind the wheel, leave shipping papers in the driver's door pouch or on the driver's seat.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.10 Where to Keep Shipping Papers and Emergency Response Information

question: How must hazardous materials shipping papers be distinguished from other papers?
choice_a: By printing them on colored paper only
choice_b: By tabbing them or keeping them on top of the stack of papers
choice_c: By stapling them to the bill of lading
choice_d: By keeping them in a separate vehicle
explanation: The manual states you must clearly distinguish hazardous materials shipping papers from others by tabbing them or keeping them on top of the stack of papers, so others can find them quickly after a crash.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.10 Where to Keep Shipping Papers and Emergency Response Information

question: Where must emergency response information for a hazardous materials shipment be kept?
choice_a: At the carrier's home terminal only
choice_b: With the shipper, not the driver
choice_c: In the same location as the shipping paper
choice_d: In a sealed envelope in the trailer
explanation: The manual states that emergency response information must be kept in the same location as the shipping paper.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.10 Where to Keep Shipping Papers and Emergency Response Information

question: A carrier must give each driver transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives a copy of which regulation, along with written instructions and a signed receipt?
choice_a: The state's commercial vehicle code
choice_b: OSHA General Industry Standards
choice_c: The EPA Clean Air Act
choice_d: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSR), Part 397
explanation: The manual states a carrier must give each driver transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives a copy of FMCSR, Part 397, along with written instructions, and drivers must sign a receipt for these documents.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.10 Where to Keep Shipping Papers and Emergency Response Information

question: How close to the traveled part of the road may you never park a vehicle carrying Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives?
choice_a: Within one hundred feet
choice_b: Within fifty feet
choice_c: Within ten feet
choice_d: Within five feet
explanation: The manual states you should never park with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives within five feet of the traveled part of the road.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.1 Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: Except for short periods needed for vehicle operation necessities like fueling, how far must you avoid parking a vehicle carrying Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives from a bridge, tunnel, building, place where people gather, or open fire?
choice_a: 500 feet
choice_b: 300 feet
choice_c: 150 feet
choice_d: 100 feet
explanation: The manual states that except for short periods needed for vehicle operation necessities such as fueling, you should not park within 300 feet of a bridge, tunnel, building, a place where people gather, or an open fire.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.1 Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: What is a 'safe haven' as described in the manual?
choice_a: A rest area located more than ten miles from a city
choice_b: A fenced area on the driver's own property
choice_c: An approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives, usually designated by local authorities
choice_d: Any truck stop with security cameras
explanation: The manual defines a safe haven as an approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives, with designation usually made by local authorities.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.1 Parking with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: For a placarded vehicle not laden with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, how close to the traveled part of the road may you park if your work requires it?
choice_a: Only if parked on a public street overnight
choice_b: Within five feet, only briefly
choice_c: Any distance, as long as flashers are on
choice_d: Never closer than 50 feet
explanation: The manual states you may park a placarded vehicle not laden with explosives within five feet of the traveled part of the road only if your work requires it, and only briefly, and someone must always watch the vehicle.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.2 Parking a Placarded Vehicle Not Transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 Explosives

question: A person attending a placarded parked vehicle who is not inside the vehicle must be within how many feet of it and have it within clear view?
choice_a: 50 feet
choice_b: 25 feet
choice_c: 200 feet
choice_d: 100 feet
explanation: The manual requires the attendant to be in the vehicle, awake, and not in the sleeper berth, or within 100 feet of the vehicle with it in clear view.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.3 Attending Parked Vehicles

question: If your vehicle breaks down and you need to use stopped vehicle signals, what should you use instead of flares?
choice_a: Burning fuses
choice_b: Reflective triangles or red electric lights
choice_c: A handheld signal mirror
choice_d: Road flares placed 100 feet apart
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to use reflective triangles or red electric lights, and never burning signals such as flares or fuses.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.4 No Flares!

question: Near what type of tank should you never use burning signals such as flares or fuses, whether the tank is loaded or empty?
choice_a: A tank used for Class 3 (Flammable Liquids) or Division 2.1 (Flammable Gas)
choice_b: A water tank
choice_c: A tank used for Class 8 (Corrosives) only
choice_d: Any tank, but only when fully loaded
explanation: The manual specifically prohibits burning signals near a tank used for Class 3 (Flammable Liquids) or Division 2.1 (Flammable Gas), whether loaded or empty.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.4 No Flares!

question: When placarded, what should a driver do regarding heavily populated areas, crowds, tunnels, narrow streets, and alleys?
choice_a: There are no restrictions as long as placards are displayed correctly
choice_b: Drive through them quickly to minimize exposure time
choice_c: Avoid them, taking other routes even if inconvenient, unless there is no other way
choice_d: Only avoid them during business hours
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to avoid heavily populated areas, crowds, tunnels, narrow streets, and alleys, taking other routes even if inconvenient, unless there is no other way.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.5 Route Restrictions

question: If transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, what must the driver have and follow?
choice_a: A verbal agreement with dispatch only
choice_b: GPS tracking enabled at all times, but no written plan required
choice_c: Nothing special beyond normal shipping papers
choice_d: A written route plan
explanation: The manual requires that if transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, you must have a written route plan and follow that plan; carriers prepare it in advance, or the driver may plan it if picking up explosives away from the terminal.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.5 Route Restrictions

question: How close may you smoke to a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (Flammable Liquids) or Division 2.1 (Gases)?
choice_a: 10 feet is acceptable
choice_b: There is no restriction if the windows are up
choice_c: 50 feet is required only at night
choice_d: You must not smoke within 25 feet of it
explanation: The manual prohibits smoking within 25 feet of a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (flammable liquids) or Division 2.1 (gases), and also within 25 feet of any vehicle carrying Class 1, 3, 4.1, 4.2, or 5 materials.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.6 No Smoking

question: Before fueling a motor vehicle containing hazardous materials, what must the driver do, and who must be at the nozzle?
choice_a: Notify the shipper by phone; no one needs to be at the nozzle
choice_b: Turn off the engine; someone must always be at the nozzle controlling fuel flow
choice_c: Remove the placards temporarily; anyone may operate the nozzle
choice_d: Turn on emergency flashers only; the nozzle can be left unattended briefly
explanation: The manual states to turn off your engine before fueling a motor vehicle containing hazardous materials, and someone must always be at the nozzle, controlling fuel flow.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.7 Refuel with Engine Off

question: What UL rating fire extinguisher must the power unit of a placarded vehicle have?
choice_a: 20 A:B:C or more
choice_b: No specific rating is required
choice_c: 10 B:C or more
choice_d: 5 B:C or more
explanation: The manual specifies that the power unit of placarded vehicles must have a fire extinguisher with a UL rating of 10 B:C or more.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.8 10 B C Fire Extinguisher

question: How often must you examine each tire on a motor vehicle carrying hazardous materials, and what is the only acceptable way to check pressure?
choice_a: Once a month, by visual inspection
choice_b: At the beginning of each trip and each time the vehicle is parked, using a tire pressure gauge
choice_c: Only when a tire appears visibly flat, by kicking the tire
choice_d: Weekly, by feeling the tire with your hand
explanation: The manual requires examining each tire at the beginning of each trip and each time the vehicle is parked, and states the only acceptable way to check tire pressure is with a tire pressure gauge.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.9 Check Tires

question: If you discover an overheated tire while transporting hazardous materials, what should you do?
choice_a: Rotate it to a different axle and continue the trip
choice_b: Pour water on it and continue driving
choice_c: Deflate it slightly and continue at reduced speed
choice_d: Remove it, place it a safe distance from the vehicle, and don't drive until the cause of overheating is corrected
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to remove an overheated tire, place it a safe distance from the vehicle, and not drive until the cause of the overheating is corrected.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.9 Check Tires

question: A driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks must have what type of equipment in the vehicle?
choice_a: A chemical shower system
choice_b: Only a standard first aid kit
choice_c: An approved gas mask and an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings
choice_d: A hazmat suit and breathing apparatus for two people
explanation: The manual requires a driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks to have an approved gas mask and an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings on the cargo tank.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.11 Equipment for Chlorine

question: How far before a railroad crossing must a placarded vehicle, or one carrying any amount of chlorine, stop?
choice_a: 100 to 150 feet
choice_b: 50 to 100 feet
choice_c: 15 to 50 feet
choice_d: 5 to 15 feet
explanation: The manual states you must stop 15 to 50 feet before the nearest rail and proceed only when sure no train is coming and you can clear the tracks without stopping.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.6.12 Stop before Railroad Crossings

question: What is the Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG), according to the manual?
choice_a: A list of approved hazmat routes in New Mexico
choice_b: A shipping company's internal safety handbook
choice_c: A driver training manual for obtaining a hazmat endorsement
choice_d: A Department of Transportation guidebook for firefighters, police, and industry workers on protecting themselves and the public from hazardous materials
explanation: The manual describes the ERG as a Department of Transportation guidebook for firefighters, police, and industry workers on how to protect themselves and the public from hazardous materials.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.1 Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)

question: The ERG is indexed by what two things, which emergency personnel look for on the shipping paper?
choice_a: Driver's name and license plate number
choice_b: Weight and dimensions of the cargo
choice_c: Insurance carrier and policy number
choice_d: Proper shipping name and hazardous materials identification number
explanation: The manual states the ERG is indexed by proper shipping name and hazardous materials identification number, which is why the proper shipping name, ID number, label, and placards on the shipping paper must be correct.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.1 Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)

question: At the scene of a crash or incident, what is a commercial driver's job regarding the spread of hazardous material?
choice_a: Wait for the shipper's approval before doing anything
choice_b: Ignore the spill and focus only on injured people
choice_c: Always attempt to contain the spill personally regardless of risk
choice_d: Limit the spread of material, only if you can safely do so
explanation: The manual lists limiting the spread of material, only if you can safely do so, as one of the driver's responsibilities at a crash scene, along with keeping people away and providing shipping papers to responders.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.2 Crashes/Incidents

question: Should a commercial driver attempt to fight a hazardous materials fire?
choice_a: Only if the fire is smaller than a car
choice_b: Yes, always, using the vehicle's fire extinguisher
choice_c: No, unless you have the training and equipment to do so safely
choice_d: Only at night when visibility of flames is better
explanation: The manual states that unless you have the training and equipment to do so safely, you should not fight hazardous materials fires, since dealing with them requires special training and protective gear.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires

question: Before opening trailer doors when you suspect a cargo fire, what should you do?
choice_a: Open them immediately to let smoke escape
choice_b: Spray water directly on the doors before opening
choice_c: Kick the doors open to check quickly
choice_d: Feel the doors to see if they are hot; if hot, do not open them
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to feel trailer doors to see if they are hot before opening them; opening hot doors lets air in and may make the fire flare up, while without air many fires only smolder until firefighters arrive.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires

question: If you discover a cargo leak, how should you attempt to identify the leaking hazardous material?
choice_a: By touching the substance carefully
choice_b: By tasting a small sample
choice_c: Using shipping papers, labels, or package location, never by touch or smell
choice_d: By smelling for chemical odors
explanation: The manual instructs identifying leaking hazardous materials using shipping papers, labels, or package location, and never touching the material or trying to identify it by smell, since toxic gases can destroy your sense of smell and injure or kill you.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires

question: Should you continue driving with hazardous materials leaking from your vehicle in order to find a phone or help?
choice_a: Yes, but only for less than one mile
choice_b: Yes, finding help quickly is the priority
choice_c: Only if the leak is a Class 9 material
choice_d: Never continue driving with hazardous materials leaking in order to find a phone, truck stop, or similar reason
explanation: The manual explicitly states never to continue driving with hazardous materials leaking from your vehicle in order to find a phone, truck stop, help, or similar reason, because the carrier pays for costly cleanup of contaminated areas.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires

question: When sending someone for help at a hazmat incident, which of the following pieces of information should you give them?
choice_a: The purchase price of the cargo
choice_b: Your name, the carrier's name, and the name of the community or city where your terminal is located
choice_c: The manufacturer's warranty details for the truck
choice_d: Your home address
explanation: The manual lists giving your name, the carrier's name, and the name of the community or city where your terminal is located, along with a description of the emergency and your exact location, as information to send with someone for help.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.3 Fires

question: If your vehicle carrying explosives is involved in a collision requiring separation of vehicles, how far should the explosives be placed from the vehicles and occupied buildings?
choice_a: At least 500 feet
choice_b: At least 50 feet
choice_c: At least 100 feet
choice_d: At least 200 feet
explanation: The manual instructs removing all explosives before separating vehicles involved in a collision and placing them at least 200 feet from the vehicles and occupied buildings, then staying a safe distance away.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards (Class 1)

question: If compressed gas is leaking from your vehicle in an accident, who must you notify?
choice_a: The nearest hospital
choice_b: No notification is required if no injuries occurred
choice_c: The shipper
choice_d: Only the vehicle's insurance company
explanation: The manual states you must notify the shipper if compressed gas is involved in any accident.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards (Class 2)

question: A vehicle involved in a leak of Division 2.3 (Poison Gases) or Division 6.1 (Poisons) must undergo what before being used again?
choice_a: A full engine overhaul
choice_b: It must be checked for stray poison
choice_c: A new paint job to cover placards
choice_d: Nothing special is required
explanation: The manual states that a vehicle involved in a leak of Division 2.3 or Division 6.1 materials must be checked for stray poison before being used again.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards (Class 6)

question: If a Division 6.2 (Infectious Substances) package appears damaged during handling, what should you do?
choice_a: Repackage it yourself and continue the delivery
choice_b: Discard the package to avoid liability
choice_c: Accept it if the damage looks minor
choice_d: Immediately contact your supervisor; damaged or leaking packages should not be accepted
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to immediately contact their supervisor if a Division 6.2 package is damaged, and states that packages appearing damaged or showing signs of leakage should not be accepted.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards (Class 6)

question: If radioactive material is involved in a leak or broken package, what should you avoid doing?
choice_a: Reporting it to your supervisor
choice_b: Photographing it
choice_c: Marking its location with cones
choice_d: Touching or inhaling the material
explanation: The manual instructs drivers not to touch or inhale radioactive material in a leak or broken package, and not to use the vehicle until it is cleaned and checked with a survey meter.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards (Class 7)

question: If a vehicle's parts are exposed to a corrosive liquid spill during transportation, what must be done?
choice_a: They must be thoroughly washed with water, and the interior washed out before reloading
choice_b: They should be sprayed with a flammable solvent
choice_c: They should be wiped with a dry cloth only
choice_d: Nothing; corrosives evaporate on their own
explanation: The manual states that parts of the vehicle exposed to a corrosive liquid must be thoroughly washed with water, and after unloading, the interior washed out as soon as possible before reloading.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.4 Responses to Specific Hazards (Class 8)

question: Which organization maintains a 24-hour toll-free line to help coordinate emergency response to chemical hazards and serves as a resource to police and firefighters?
choice_a: The state Department of Revenue
choice_b: The National Response Center
choice_c: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration
choice_d: The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration
explanation: The manual describes the National Response Center as helping coordinate emergency response to chemical hazards and maintaining a 24-hour toll-free line (800-424-8802) as a resource to police and firefighters.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: How long must the general public be evacuated, or a major transportation artery closed, before notification of the National Response Center is required?
choice_a: More than 15 minutes
choice_b: More than 24 hours
choice_c: More than one hour
choice_d: More than 30 minutes
explanation: The manual states notification is required when the general public is evacuated for more than one hour, or a major transportation artery or facility is closed for one hour or more.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: A release of a marine pollutant must be reported to the National Response Center if it exceeds what quantity for a liquid?
choice_a: 50 gallons
choice_b: 1,000 gallons
choice_c: 500 gallons
choice_d: 119 gallons
explanation: The manual specifies that a marine pollutant release must be reported if it exceeds 119 gallons for a liquid, or 882 pounds for a solid.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: What is CHEMTREC's purpose, according to the manual?
choice_a: To collect fines for hazmat violations
choice_b: To issue hazmat endorsements to drivers
choice_c: To provide emergency personnel with technical information about the physical properties of hazardous materials
choice_d: To manufacture emergency response equipment
explanation: The manual explains that CHEMTREC, based in Washington and reachable 24 hours toll-free, was created to provide emergency personnel with technical information about the physical properties of hazardous materials, and works in close communication with the National Response Center.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: When telephoning the National Response Center to report an incident, what information should the caller be ready to give?
choice_a: Only the vehicle's VIN number
choice_b: The driver's Social Security number
choice_c: Only the make and model of the truck
choice_d: Their name, the carrier's name and address, phone number, date/time/location of the incident, and extent of injuries
explanation: The manual lists the caller's name, the carrier's name and address, a phone number, the date, time, and location of the incident, and the extent of injuries as information to provide to the National Response Center.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.7.5 Required Notification

question: Hazardous materials are categorized into how many major hazard classes, plus additional categories for consumer commodities and combustible liquids?
choice_a: Seven
choice_b: Eight
choice_c: Nine
choice_d: Ten
explanation: The manual states hazardous materials are categorized into nine major hazard classes, with additional categories for consumer commodities and combustible liquids.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, Classes of Hazardous Materials (Figure 9.11)

question: According to the manual's hazard class table, which class is designated for Corrosives, with examples such as hydrochloric acid and battery fluid?
choice_a: Class 6
choice_b: Class 9
choice_c: Class 7
choice_d: Class 8
explanation: The manual's hazard class table lists Class 8 as Corrosives, with examples such as hydrochloric acid and battery fluid.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, Figure 9.11 Hazard Class Definitions

question: Per the glossary in 49 CFR 171.8, what is 'bulk packaging'?
choice_a: Packaging under 50 pounds with no capacity threshold
choice_b: Any wooden crate used for shipping
choice_c: Packaging, other than a vessel or barge, in which hazardous materials are loaded with no intermediate form of containment and which exceeds specified capacity or mass thresholds (such as more than 450 L as a receptacle for a liquid)
choice_d: A packaging designed to hold exactly one gallon
explanation: The glossary defines bulk packaging as packaging, other than a vessel or barge, including a transport vehicle or freight container, in which hazardous materials are loaded with no intermediate form of containment and which exceeds thresholds such as a maximum capacity greater than 450 L (119 gallons) for a liquid.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary (49 CFR 171.8)

question: According to the glossary, what defines a 'cargo tank' under 49 CFR 171.8?
choice_a: A tank used exclusively for drinking water
choice_b: A bulk packaging that is a tank intended primarily for the carriage of liquids or gases and is permanently attached to, or forms a part of, a motor vehicle
choice_c: Any container weighing more than 50 pounds
choice_d: A packaging with a capacity of less than 5 gallons
explanation: The glossary defines a cargo tank as bulk packaging intended primarily for carrying liquids or gases, permanently attached to or forming part of a motor vehicle, and not fabricated under a cylinder, portable tank, or tank car specification.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary

topic: Hazardous Materials Glossary - Carrier and Consignee
question: How does the glossary define 'Consignee'?
choice_a: The government inspector who certifies the shipment
choice_b: The person who loads the shipment onto the vehicle
choice_c: The business or person to whom a shipment is delivered
choice_d: The driver responsible for the shipment
explanation: The glossary defines consignee as the business or person to whom a shipment is delivered, while a carrier is defined as a person who transports passengers or property in commerce by rail car, aircraft, motor vehicle, or vessel.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary

question: How does the glossary define 'Hazard class'?
choice_a: The insurance risk category assigned by underwriters
choice_b: A number from 1 to 100 rating the danger level
choice_c: The weight class of the vehicle carrying the material
choice_d: The category of hazard assigned to a hazardous material under defining criteria; a material may meet the criteria for more than one class but is assigned to only one
explanation: The glossary states hazard class is the category of hazard assigned under the defining criteria of Part 173 and the Sec. 172.101 Table, and that a material may meet the defining criteria for more than one hazard class but is assigned to only one.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary

question: What is the 'Shipper's certification' as described in the glossary?
choice_a: A receipt proving payment for freight charges
choice_b: The shipper's insurance policy number
choice_c: A statement on a shipping paper, signed by the shipper, certifying that the shipment was properly classified, described, packaged, marked, and labeled according to applicable regulations
choice_d: A government-issued permit required before any shipment departs
explanation: The glossary describes the shipper's certification as a statement on a shipping paper, signed by the shipper, saying he or she prepared the shipment properly according to law, including that the materials are properly classified, described, packaged, marked, and labeled.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary

question: What does the glossary define as a 'Portable tank'?
choice_a: A tank car used exclusively on railroads
choice_b: A tank permanently welded to the vehicle frame
choice_c: Any container that a single person can carry by hand
choice_d: Bulk packaging designed primarily to be loaded onto, or temporarily attached to, a transport vehicle or ship, and equipped with skids, mountings, or accessories for mechanical handling
explanation: The glossary defines portable tank as bulk packaging designed primarily to be loaded onto or temporarily attached to a transport vehicle or ship, equipped with skids, mountings, or accessories to facilitate handling by mechanical means, excluding cargo tanks, tank cars, and certain cylinders.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary

topic: Hazardous Materials Glossary - Proper Shipping Name
question: What is the 'Proper shipping name' as defined in the glossary?
choice_a: Any nickname commonly used by shippers
choice_b: The name of the hazardous materials shown in Roman print (not italics) in Sec. 172.101
choice_c: The chemical formula of the substance
choice_d: The brand name printed on the packaging
explanation: The glossary defines proper shipping name as the name of the hazardous materials shown in Roman print (not italics) in Sec. 172.101.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary

question: What is a 'Reportable quantity (RQ)' according to the glossary?
choice_a: The total weight of the vehicle's cargo
choice_b: Any quantity greater than 500 pounds
choice_c: The amount of material that must be reported to the shipper daily
choice_d: The quantity specified in Column 2 of the Appendix to Sec. 172.101 for any material identified in Column 1
explanation: The glossary defines reportable quantity (RQ) as the quantity specified in Column 2 of the Appendix to Sec. 172.101 for any material identified in Column 1 of the Appendix.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary

question: What does the manual say about being tested on the Hazardous Materials Glossary itself?
choice_a: You will be tested on every definition in the glossary
choice_b: The glossary is tested only on the hazmat endorsement exam, not the general knowledge test
choice_c: The manual notes you will not be tested on this glossary
choice_d: Only the definitions of 'carrier' and 'consignee' are testable
explanation: The manual explicitly notes, 'You will not be tested on this glossary,' immediately before presenting the definitions drawn from 49 CFR 171.8.
source_note: NM CDL Manual, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, 9.8 Hazardous Materials Glossary
